guides.title: Basket or oven-style air fryer: what should you compare?
guides.deck: Start with the food you cook on a busy Tuesday, not with the shape on the box. Then let the shape follow.
guides.description: A plain-English comparison of basket-style and oven-style air fryers: what each shape does well, what to check before you choose, and how the appliances we track blur the line.

body.alt: Illustration comparing a rounded basket-style air fryer and a taller oven-style air fryer with a door and rack, side by side on a shelf
body.caption: Illustration: AI-generated for this site. It shows the two shapes, not any specific product we track.

body.text: Most buying advice starts with capacity or wattage. Start one step earlier: with the meals you actually cook. The two air fryer shapes are good at different things, and the shape you pick quietly decides your weeknight routine.
What a basket style does best

A basket air fryer is a drawer you shake. That is the whole magic. Fries crisp because you pull the drawer, give everything a toss, and push it back in. Cleanup is usually one nonstick basket, and preheating is quick because you are heating a small chamber. If your air fryer life is frozen fries, chicken pieces, roasted vegetables for two to four people, the basket shape fits.

The trade-offs show up when dinner gets big. Two levels of food compete for one drawer. Anything breaded and delicate can be awkward to flip without losing coating. And a tall drawer of food cooks less evenly than a shallow layer, so big batches want a shake you might not have time for.
What an oven style does best

An oven-style air fryer trades the drawer for a door, racks, and usually more room. You can run two levels at once, rotate trays halfway through, and fit irregular things a drawer would refuse: a whole chicken piece with bones, a small casserole, skewers. Many double as toaster ovens, which means they earn their counter space at breakfast too.

The costs are the mirror image. Doors release heat and smell into the kitchen. Racks and trays mean more pieces to wash, and the machine is usually taller and deeper, so cabinet clearance matters more. If you hate washing dishes, count the accessories before you fall for the capacity.
The four questions worth answering first

headers: Points you toward an oven style
rows: How many people do you cook for on most nights?
One to four; shallow layers cook best
Five or more, or two levels running at once
What is your cleanup tolerance?
One basket, ideally dishwasher-safe
You accept racks, trays, and a crumb tray
Where will it live?
Under a cabinet; modest footprint
Needs standing height clearance and door swing room
Do you want it to replace a toaster?
No; it is a single-purpose tool
Yes; many oven styles toast and bake too

body.text: One honest warning about the labels

As we built the product shelf on this site, we noticed the naming gets blurry. One appliance we track is titled with both words: it is described as a dual-basket unit and as an oven, with windows on the baskets. Marketing borrows the strengths of both shapes, so the label on the box will not settle your decision. The listing pages will, if you look at the photos and the basket arrangement rather than the headline.
Questions to take with you

items: Does the basket or oven cavity match the deepest food you cook, not just the biggest?
Are the pieces that touch food removable and dishwasher-safe, or hand-wash only?
How far does the door or drawer extend when open, and does that fit your counter?
If it promises multiple functions, which two or three will you actually use weekly?

body.label: See the appliances we are tracking
body.text: Every row on our shop table links to the observed Amazon listing, with the sources we read.

items.q: Is one shape always healthier?
items.a: No. Both shapes cook with moving hot air. Health claims belong to what you cook, not to the shape of the machine.

items.q: Is a dual-basket model the same as two air fryers?
items.a: It is two baskets sharing one housing and one plug. Independent controls help when you want two foods finishing at different times, but check whether temperatures can actually differ between baskets before assuming it.

items.q: Which shape should a first-time buyer pick?
items.a: The shape that matches your most common meal. If you cannot name that meal yet, a mid-size basket model is the cheaper way to find out whether the habit sticks.

guides.summary: Choose from the meal, not from the box. A basket drawer is one shakeable layer that suits frozen and crisp foods for a small household; an oven-style unit buys rack positions and a door at the cost of counter depth and more pieces to wash. Four questions settle it in about a minute.

guides.title: A no-hype checklist for comparing air fryer capacity
guides.deck: Capacity is the first number you see and the easiest one to misread. Here is how to read it better.
guides.description: What quart ratings measure, what they leave out, and a printable checklist of questions to compare air fryer capacity without the marketing gloss.

body.alt: Illustration of two cooking baskets of different sizes filled to different levels, with a measuring cup and kitchen scale
body.caption: Illustration: AI-generated for this site. Numbers in listings, not in artwork, are what count.

body.text: Quarts sell air fryers. They are also the least self-explanatory number in the kitchen aisle, because a quart measures volume, not dinner. Four quarts of air is not four quarts of fries. This checklist gives you the questions that actually predict whether an air fryer feeds your household.
Why the number on the box misleads

Capacity is measured to the walls of the basket. Your food does not touch the walls, and it should not: hot air needs room to move around each piece for crisping. Pile food to the ceiling of the basket and you get steaming, not frying, no matter what the quart rating promised. Usable capacity is always smaller than stated capacity, and the gap widens with anything bulky or irregular.

Shape matters as much as volume. A wide, shallow basket crisps a single layer better than a tall, narrow one of the same rated volume, because more food sits near the heating element and the fan. Two smaller baskets can beat one larger number for cooking two things at once, if the controls let you run them independently.
The checklist

rows: Name the main dish you will cook most
Capacity needs are set by your signature meal, not by the largest one you can imagine
Look at basket shape, not just quarts
Shallow and wide crisps single layers; tall and narrow stacks heat unevenly
Check the height of the basket, not just floor area
A roast or a layered dish needs vertical room, a tray of fries does not
Count how many layers you would really run
Stacked cooking means rotating or shaking mid-cook; decide if you will actually do that
Measure the counter footprint and the open-drawer depth
The drawer extends when open; the machine needs that space every time you use it
Read the dishwasher claims for every removable piece
One dishwasher-safe basket is a different life than four hand-washed accessories

body.text: How the numbers in our own shelf read

The appliances we track make a good case study in reading titles carefully. As of the date we observed them, one listing title leads with 6 quart and splits that space across two independent 3-quart baskets. Another leads with 8 Qt and a single extra-large basket. A third, an oven-style unit, leads with 26QT of cavity. Those are not comparable numbers, and they are not meant to be: one measures drawer space split in two, one measures a single basket, and one measures a whole oven interior.

Notice also what the titles do with temperature: one advertises a 450°F high-heat setting. That is a feature claim from the listing, not something we have measured. We do not repeat pricing or rating numbers on this site, and we treat listing-title specifications as claims to verify on the listing page, not as established facts.

One warning from our own register: for the tracked 8-quart unit, the Amazon listing and the manufacturer's own page describe two different machines, and the listing shows two different temperature ranges in two places (flags FLG-026 and FLG-027 on our Flagged for review page). A quart figure printed on a box is only as reliable as the consistency of the pages behind it. When a listing and the maker disagree, treat the spec as unresolved and check the model number before you buy.
A rule of thumb for households

items: Cooking for one or two most nights: a single-basket model in the middle of the line's range usually fits, with room to host occasionally.
Cooking for three or four with picky eaters: two independent baskets earn their footprint when the two foods need different times or temperatures.
Batch cooking, big families, or replacing a toaster: look at oven styles and judge by tray size and rack count rather than one big quart figure.

body.label: Compare the tracked models
body.text: The shop table shows the observed listing for each tracked appliance, side by side, with the exact title we read.

items.q: Does a bigger air fryer use much more electricity?
items.a: Larger cavities generally draw more power to reach temperature, but total energy depends on cook time and how full you run it. A big machine running a small batch can waste energy; a right-sized machine used daily may not. We have not measured any unit, so treat this as physics reasoning, not lab data.

items.q: Are quart ratings standardized across brands?
items.a: No single standard governs where brands measure from, which is exactly why basket shape and your signature meal should outrank the number.

items.q: Is a 26-quart oven the same as a 26-quart basket fryer?
items.a: No. The oven figure describes the whole cavity including space around racks; the basket figure describes the drawer. Treat them as different units of meaning.

guides.summary: Quarts are not comparable across shapes: one 6-quart figure can be two 3-quart baskets or one 6-quart drawer, and a maker's quart count says nothing about the food you can actually fit. Read the chamber shape, the maker's own serving line and the outside dimensions, and treat a capacity claim with no source as a marketing number.

guides.title: How to assess cleanup and counter-space trade-offs
guides.deck: The best-looking appliance is the one you will actually clean, and the one that still fits when the drawer is open.
guides.description: A practical method for weighing dishwasher claims, hand-washing reality, counter footprint, ventilation clearance and open-door space before you buy a kitchen appliance.

body.alt: Illustration of a sponge, a drying rack with washed baskets, and a measuring tape across a wooden countertop
body.caption: Illustration: AI-generated for this site.

body.text: Appliance regret almost never comes from cooking performance. It comes from the two taxes you pay every single day: the washing, and the space. Both are predictable before you buy, if you ask the right questions.
The cleanup questions, in order
1. Count the pieces that touch food

A basket fryer is one basket and maybe a crisper plate. An oven-style unit can be two racks, a fry basket, a crumb tray, and a rotisserie spit. Every piece that touched grease needs washing after every greasy cook. Before you buy, list the removable parts from the listing photos and imagine the drying rack after taco night.
2. Read dishwasher claims precisely

Titles are careful with this, and so should you be. On our shelf, one observed listing titles its two baskets as dishwasher-safe, and another titles a single nonstick basket the same way. Neither phrase tells you whether racks, trays, or the housing wipe down easily; it only covers named pieces. Nonstick also has a service life: metal utensils and abrasive sponges shorten it, so the claim survives only as long as your habits are gentle.
3. Judge the grease path

Grease lands where the air ends. In basket units it pools under a removable basket, which is convenient. In oven styles it can drip toward the door and the crumb tray, which is a wider wipe. Door glass, interior walls, and heating-element guards all earn a spot on the cleaning schedule eventually. Look at interior photos for how far food spatter can travel.
The counter-space questions

rows: Footprint
Width and depth of the base, plus vibration room at the back
The back needs ventilation clearance, not just the sides
Open clearance
Depth of the drawer or door swing in use
You open it while cooking, so the space must be free at dinner time, not just in the store photo
Height
Machine height plus anything you place on top now
Cabinet overhangs and shelves above eat usable height
Weight
Check the listing's shipping weight as a proxy
Heavy units do not move for cleaning behind and under, and that chore matters

body.text: One trick that saves returns: outline the machine's footprint in painter's tape on the counter, then outline the open drawer in front of it. Live with the tape for two days. Most people discover the open-drawer outline crosses either the sink or the stove, and that discovery is cheaper in tape than in shipping.
The trade-off, stated plainly

Big capacity buys you fewer cooking batches and costs you more washing and more counter. Small capacity keeps cleanup to one basket and gives the counter back, at the price of cooking in rounds. Neither is wrong; the mistake is paying for capacity you use twice a year while washing the price of it every night.

body.label: See what each tracked unit claims
body.text: The shop table preserves each observed listing title, so you can compare dishwasher and accessory claims in one place.

items.q: Do I need to clean the heating element?
items.a: Follow the manual's guidance for the specific unit. What we can say generally: grease reaches the area above the food chamber over time, and units designed with easier access to that area make the deep clean less of a project.

items.q: Is dishwasher-safe the same as durable?
items.a: No. Dishwasher-safe describes surviving the wash; nonstick coatings still age with abrasive contact. Gentle washing extends the life of any coated piece.

items.q: Can I store the appliance in a cabinet?
items.a: Yes, if you will actually lift it in and out. Weight is the deciding factor, which is why we suggest checking listing weight before choosing an under-cabinet life.

guides.summary: The two daily costs of an air fryer are the pieces you wash and the counter it occupies. Count the accessories before you fall for the capacity, measure the outside box rather than the advertised volume, and check which part of the washing claim the maker actually states.

guides.title: Questions to ask before buying a multi-function kitchen appliance
guides.deck: Multi-function appliances promise a dozen tools in one box. Ask which three you will actually use.
guides.description: A buyer's interrogation guide for combination air fryers, toaster ovens and other multi-function appliances: counting real functions, presets, accessories and the learning curve.

body.alt: Illustration of a countertop oven with small floating icons suggesting different cooking modes
body.caption: Illustration: AI-generated for this site.

body.text: Every appliance category eventually grows a multi-function flagship, and kitchen gear is no exception. The pitch is seductive: air fryer, toaster, oven, dehydrator, rotisserie, broiler, one plug. The reality, for most households, is that three functions do ninety-five percent of the work. Your job is to find out which three, and whether this box does them well.
Count the presets, then discount them

Presets are recipes, not features. One appliance we track advertises twenty-four one-touch preset options in its title; the number reads impressively, but think about what it means. You do not need twenty-four buttons to cook twenty-four foods. You need a temperature, a time, and the judgment to check early. Presets earn their keep for foods you cook on repeat; the rest are shortcuts you will never press. When you compare units, ignore the count and hunt for the presets matching your weekly foods.

A check we now run on every tracked appliance: the preset and accessory counts on the tracked 26-quart unit differ across official pages (flag FLG-024). Count from the listing's own spec table, and treat round numbers in marketing copy as marketing.
The accessory audit

Functions are delivered by accessories, and accessories are delivered by you to the sink. A rotisserie function implies a spit, forks, and a removal tool. Dehydrating implies racks, and hours of low heat that occupy the machine. Baking implies a pan or tray. One observed listing on our shelf titles six cooking accessories as included, which sounds generous until you imagine all six in the dishwasher. Ask for each advertised function: what physical part does it need, where does that part store, and who washes it.
Five questions before you buy

items: Which three functions will I use in a normal week? Name the meals, not the modes.
Does each of those functions have a dedicated, well-reviewed control path, or is it buried in a combo mode with compromises?
What accessories does each function require, and are they included or extra purchases?
How big is the learning curve, and does the manual (available as a PDF on most listings) read like a cookbook or a contract?
Where do the accessories live between uses? Storage is the silent dealbreaker for combo appliances.

body.text: When a multi-function box is the right call

Combination appliances shine in three situations: small kitchens where three separate machines cannot fit; households that genuinely use the spread, like one person toasting at breakfast and air-frying at dinner; and renters or temporary setups where one box beats a move of many. If that is not your life, the honest math favors two good single-purpose tools over one crowd-pleasing box, even when the box looks like the better deal on paper.

One more angle from our shelf: the multi-function units we track sit in the same observed category (air fryers) as the basket models, but they are judged by buyers differently, on toast quality and oven evenness as much as frying. If you buy a combo unit, expect to judge it as an oven first; that is where most daily use lands.

body.label: Review the multi-function units we track
body.text: Each row links to the observed listing so you can run this interrogation against the real spec sheet.

items.q: Do combo appliances cook worse than dedicated units?
items.a: They can, at the edges: a combo oven's air fry mode shares a cavity designed for baking, so crisping a single layer may take more attention than a dedicated basket. For most daily cooking the difference is manageable; for fries-every-night households it is the trade to test.

items.q: Is more presets better?
items.a: More presets is more buttons. The useful count is how many presets match foods you already cook weekly.

items.q: What is the first function to skip?
items.a: For most buyers: dehydrating or rotisserie. Both are occasional-use modes that carry permanent accessory storage and washing costs.

guides.summary: A multi-function appliance pays for itself only if you use more than one of its functions. Ask which modes carry a stated temperature range, which ones you would have used last month, and whether the panel lets you set time and heat by hand - that decides whether it replaces two appliances or adds one more.

guides.title: Is your meat thermometer telling you the right number?
guides.deck: A thermometer is only as useful as the number you compare it with, and the place you stick the probe.
guides.description: How to use a meat thermometer so the reading means something: USDA target temperatures, probe placement, calibration checks, and what wireless specs like range and probe count really buy you.

body.alt: Illustration of a digital probe thermometer with a cable beside a roast on a cutting board
body.caption: Illustration: AI-generated for this site.

body.text: An instrument is only trustworthy if two things are true: it reads accurately, and it sits where the temperature means what you think it means. Meat thermometers fail cooks on both counts, quietly. The good news is that both are fixable with five minutes and a cup of ice water.
First, the numbers worth trusting

The USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service publishes safe minimum internal temperatures, and their chart is the reference the rest of us should quote. From that chart: beef, pork, veal and lamb steaks, chops and roasts are cooked safely at 145°F with a three-minute rest, and all poultry, including ground poultry, at 165°F. The full chart covers ground meats, fish and more; link it, bookmark it, stop guessing.

rows: Beef, pork, veal, lamb — steaks, chops, roasts
145°F plus a 3-minute rest
USDA FSIS safe temperature chart (S10)
Ground meats (beef, pork, veal, lamb)
USDA FSIS safe temperature chart (S10)
All poultry (whole or ground)
USDA FSIS safe temperature chart (S10)

body.text: Carryover heat matters too: a roast resting on the board keeps climbing a few degrees after it leaves the heat. The USDA's three-minute rest exists partly for that reason. Pulling meat exactly at the target number is a skill; pulling a few degrees early and resting is the forgiving version of the same skill.
Placement: the error nobody blames

USDA guidance on thermometers is blunt about placement: for whole poultry, check the thigh, the wing, and the thickest part of the breast, avoiding bone. The general rule for any cut is the thickest part, away from bone, fat pockets, and the pan. Bone conducts heat differently than meat, so a probe touching bone reads a temperature the meat itself does not have. A reading near the surface reads cooler than the center. Both mistakes send confident cooks back to the oven with a false number.

With thin cuts, angle the probe so the sensitive tip sits in the thermal center, not halfway through the side. With irregular cuts, take two or three readings in different spots and trust the lowest center reading; that is the coldest place your food still needs to cook.
Calibration: the five-minute check

items: Fill a glass with crushed ice and a little water, stir, and wait thirty seconds for it to settle at the ice point.
Insert the probe so the tip sits in the ice water without touching the glass.
The reading should settle near 32°F. Note how far off it is.
If your model adjusts, follow its calibration instructions; if not, remember the offset and apply it mentally, or retire the probe.
Repeat whenever the probe is dropped, and whenever readings start feeling suspicious. Drops knock probes out of true more than any other cause.

body.text: Three things our register caught while checking the tracked units against their makers' pages. The manufacturer's own pages disagree about the tracked wireless thermometer's battery life: 70+ hours on the product page, up to 60 on the FAQ, and 50 on the Amazon listing (flag FLG-023). The tracked instant-read unit's maker page is narrower than its own listing: the maker says a waterproof design with no IP code and an LCD, the listing claims IP67, an LED screen and NSF certification (flag FLG-025). And the 8 Qt fryer's maker page and listing name the same model number while disagreeing on wattage and case size (flags FLG-026, FLG-027). Conflicts like these are exactly why we link our sources instead of summarising them.
What wireless specs actually buy you

The smart thermometers now crowding the aisle add a radio and an app to the probe. Read those specs with a practical eye. Range claims are line-of-sight promises; walls, appliances and your grill lid eat them fast, so 'unlimited range' titles usually mean the signal routes through your home network rather than a direct radio link. Probe count decides how many foods or zones you can watch at once. Heat-resistance ratings tell you whether the probe survives leaving in a hot oven or grill for the whole cook.

As an example of how these claims stack in a listing title, the wireless thermometer we track advertises three ultra-thin probes, app-based range, a high heat-resistance ceiling, and multiple sensors per probe, as its title read on the day we observed it. Those are claims to check against the listing and the manual, not measurements of ours. What the specs do not change: placement discipline and the ice-water check. A wireless probe in the wrong spot reports the wrong temperature at the speed of light.

body.label: See the thermometer we are tracking
body.text: One observed listing, linked straight to Amazon, with the exact title we read.

items.q: Can I leave a probe in the meat for the whole cook?
items.a: Only if the manufacturer rates the probe for sustained oven or grill temperatures; that is what heat-resistance ratings describe. Check the manual before leaving any probe in during a long or high-heat cook.

items.q: Do I need a wireless thermometer at all?
items.a: No. An instant-read probe used correctly produces trustworthy numbers with zero setup. Wireless buys convenience and monitoring, not accuracy. Start simple if you are new to thermometers.

items.q: Where should the probe go in a whole chicken?
items.a: Per USDA guidance: check the thickest part of the breast, the thigh, and the wing, avoiding bone. The lowest of those readings is the number to cook to.

guides.summary: A thermometer is only as good as where you put it. USDA's guidance is to place it in the thickest part away from bone, fat and gristle, to check a large roast in several places, and to cook to the minimum internal temperature: 165 °F for all poultry, 160 °F for ground meats, 145 °F with a three-minute rest for whole-muscle beef, pork, veal and lamb.

guides.title: Which air fryer parts are actually dishwasher-safe?
guides.image_alt: Illustration of two dark nonstick air fryer baskets sitting on the upper rack of an open dishwasher, with a folded towel beside it
guides.deck: Cleanup is the cost you pay every day, and it is the specification most listings treat as a footnote. Here is what each maker states, in their own words, and where they stop.
guides.description: What the five products we track say about dishwasher-safe parts: which component each claim covers, which pages stay silent, and what to check in the manual before you load anything.
guides.summary: Only two of the three air fryers here publish a dishwasher claim, and both are narrow: the Chefman dual-basket listing calls its baskets nonstick and dishwasher safe, and the 8 qt Chefman page says basket and rack are top-rack dishwasher safe. The Emeril oven page states nothing about washing in the text this site reads, and ThermoMaven calls its probe 100% waterproof without mentioning a dishwasher, while CHEF iQ does state dishwasher-safe probes. A missing claim is not a permission: the parts nobody names are the parts to check in the manual.

body.text: Every buying guide tells you the capacity. Almost none of them tells you what you will be doing at 8pm with a greasy basket in your hand. So we took the one line that decides that - what the maker says may go in a dishwasher - and wrote down exactly what each official page states, including the pages that state nothing.
What each page says, stated narrowly

rows: CHEFMAN 6 Qt Dual Basket

The listing title itself carries the phrase “2 Independent 3Qt Nonstick Dishwasher Safe Frying Baskets”. The claim covers the two baskets. The register also records the maker’s own page stating the same for its nonstick baskets.
Amazon listing title, read 2026-11-20; manufacturer page for the same model
Chefman TurboFry 8 Qt (RJ38-SQSS-8T)
The manufacturer page states the basket and rack are top-rack dishwasher safe. “Top-rack” is part of the claim, not a detail.
Chefman product page for that model
Emeril Lagasse 26 QT French Door

The parts of the manufacturer page this site reads - the specification strip and the product description - make no washing statement at all: capacity, presets, fan, dimensions and voltage, and nothing about cleaning.
Emeril Everyday product page, read 2026-11-20
ThermoMaven 1 Sec probe
“Featuring a 100% waterproof design, this device easily withstands spills and scrubbing.” Waterproof, yes. Dishwasher, not stated.
ThermoMaven product page
CHEF iQ Sense probes
The manufacturer product page states the probes are waterproof and dishwasher safe. Being rated for sustained heat inside a cooker is a separate claim and is not the same permission.
CHEF iQ product page

body.text: A missing claim is not permission

It is tempting to read the Emeril row above as “the accessories are hand-wash only”. It does not say that either. What it says is that the pages we read do not answer the question - and on a product whose pitch includes a stack of accessories that come in the box, that gap is worth asking about before the first dinner, not after. Where a page is silent, this site publishes silence.

The same applies to the parts no page mentions: the housing, the heating element, the crumb tray, the door glass. None of the pages we read states whether those can be wet, so none of them is described here. The manual is the only document that speaks for the machine you will actually receive.
Three questions worth answering from the manual

items: Which component does the claim cover? “Basket” and “basket and rack” are different claims, and neither one includes the body of the machine.
Is there a rack position? The 8 qt Chefman page says top rack. That qualifier is the manufacturer limiting its own claim, so treat it as part of the claim.

Does the nonstick coating get its own sentence? All three air fryers here describe nonstick surfaces, and a coating can survive a dishwasher while the maker still recommends hand-washing to keep it. Those are two different statements.

body.text: The one number to double-check while you are there

Accessory count. The Emeril listing title says six cooking accessories are included, while the same listing's product summary mentions seven, and the manufacturer page states no count in the text we read. Neither number is published as a fact here; the disagreement is recorded and dated as FLG-024. It is a fair illustration of why this site reads pages instead of trusting a marketing line.

Nobody in this session put a basket in a dishwasher. Nothing on this page is a test result; it is a record of what five official pages state, with the date each was read. Two of them - the 8 qt Chefman page and the CHEF iQ page - were read in an earlier dated pass and are cited by their register ids; the other three were re-read on 2026-11-20 and say so in the source register.

items.q: Is dishwasher-safe the same as waterproof?
items.a: No. A waterproofing statement is about water reaching the device; a dishwasher claim is about heat, detergent and spray specifically. ThermoMaven states the first and not the second, which is why its row reads the way it does.

items.q: Why does this site not just say “yes, all of them are fine”?
items.a: Because the pages do not say that, and a wrong answer here costs you a coating or a warranty. Every claim on the site has to point at an official page, and where the official page is silent the site has to be silent too.

items.q: What about baked-on grease?
items.a: That is not a manufacturer claim on any of these pages, so it is not answered here. This page answers one question - what the maker permits - not what a particular soaking routine can survive.

body.text: The specification grid on every product page carries the washing row, with “not stated” where a maker does not state it.

guides.title: What “NIST certified” means on a thermometer
guides.image_alt: Illustration of a folding instant-read thermometer beside a magnifying glass hovering over a blank specification label
guides.deck: An accuracy figure, a certification acronym and an ingress rating tell three different stories. Only one of them is about your dinner.
guides.description: A plain-English read of the claims on a thermometer listing - NIST certification, plus or minus half a degree, an IP rating - set against what USDA FSIS says about typical accuracy and about where to put the probe.
guides.summary: The ThermoMaven page we read claims NIST-certified accuracy of ±0.5 °F on a thermocouple sensor with a one-second read; its Amazon listing title adds “NSF Certified” and “IP67 waterproof”, which the maker's own page does not state in those words. USDA's guidance, meanwhile, says most food thermometers read accurately within 2 to 4 °F. Those numbers are not rivals: one is a certified lab figure for an instrument, the other is what to expect in a kitchen.

body.text: A thermometer listing is a wall of acronyms, and each one quietly means something different. Here is the difference between the claims that appear on the two thermometer products we track, and what each of them can and cannot tell you.
“NIST certified ±0.5 °F” - what that sentence is about

The ThermoMaven product page states “NIST-certified precision, with an accuracy of ±0.5℉/±0.3℃” and describes a one-second instant read on a thermocouple sensor. Read carefully, that is a statement about the instrument measured against a reference. It is not a promise about the number you get at 6pm with the grill lid half open, because nothing in that sentence covers your technique, your placement or your meat.
USDA's number is the kitchen number

The Food Safety and Inspection Service's food thermometer factsheet says something refreshingly unglamorous: “Most food thermometers will give an accurate reading within 2 to 4 degrees F”, and “the reading will only be correct if the thermometer is placed in the proper location of the food”. That gap - half a degree on a certificate, two to four degrees at the stove - is the reason an accuracy figure should not decide your purchase on its own. Placement decides it.

body.text: Why nobody here translates “IP67” for you

There is a temptation to fill that cell with a confident sentence. We did not, for a boring reason: the rating's meaning is defined by a standard we do not hold in our source list, and the maker's own page describes a “100% waterproof design” without invoking the code. So the site publishes both statements and no interpretation of its own. If a number has to be inferred, it does not get published - that is the rule this whole project runs on, and it is the rule that keeps a specification grid honest.
The warranty sentence worth noticing

From the same manufacturer page: the lifetime warranty has to be “activated within 30 days after purchase”. A warranty with an activation window is not one you can discover in year two. If after-sales cover matters to you, check for an activation, a registration or a receipt requirement before the box goes into the loft.
Where to put the probe - the part with a source

items: Place it in the thickest part of the food, away from bone, fat or gristle (FSIS).
For thin foods, insert it through the side until it reaches the centre (FSIS).
Read the manufacturer's instructions for how far the probe must go in; if they are gone, look for the dimple on the stem that marks the end of the sensing area (FSIS).
Check every piece, and check a large or irregularly shaped roast in several places - size, quantity and how the food is stacked mean pieces reach temperature at different times (FSIS).

body.text: And the number to cook to does not come from a thermometer brand. It comes from the USDA chart: 165 °F for all poultry, 160 °F for ground meats, 145 °F with a three-minute rest for beef, pork, veal and lamb steaks, chops and roasts. That chart is worth reading once and keeping; every device recommendation is secondary to it.
Nothing here is a bench test. Every sentence traces to a manufacturer page, the observed Amazon listing, or USDA FSIS guidance, each listed below with the date it was read.

items.q: Does ±0.5 °F make a thermometer better than one rated ±2 °F?
items.a: It means the manufacturer's certified figure is tighter. In use, the FSIS range of 2 to 4 °F describes typical accuracy for the category, and a placement error is larger than the difference between those two numbers. Judge a thermometer on response time, probe length, how legible the readout is and what the warranty asks of you - then on the tolerance figure.

items.q: Is an inexpensive instant-read probe useless?
items.a: No. USDA's position is that using a food thermometer at all, correctly, is the only reliable way to confirm food has reached a safe minimum internal temperature. That sentence is about thermometers, not about expensive ones.

items.q: Why does the listing say NSF and the maker's page not say it in words?
items.a: Because two different pages, written by different people at different times, carry different copy. We record the difference instead of resolving it. That is what the flagged register is for.

guides.title: Sync Finish and Hi-Fry: what the buttons do
guides.image_alt: Illustration of a dual-basket air fryer control panel with two blank displays and a row of round touch controls
guides.deck: Dual-basket machines sell themselves on three named features. Two are about timing, one is about temperature, and none of them is about how well food cooks.
guides.description: What Sync Finish, Hi-Fry and independent baskets mean on the Chefman dual-basket air fryer, read from the manufacturer page and the Amazon listing, including the disputed temperature ceiling on the 8 qt model.
guides.summary: The manufacturer page describes the 6 qt Chefman as two air fryers in one, 3 quarts each, with Sync Finish so both baskets land at the same time and a Hi-Fry function whose maximum it states as 450 °F (235 °C). Independent baskets buy you two temperatures and two timers; they do not buy you one 6-quart chamber. And read the ceilings per model: the same brand's 8 qt page states 200-400 °F while its listing title advertises a 450 °F Hi-Fry burst, so this site publishes the lower figure for that unit and flags the disagreement.

body.text: Feature names on an appliance panel are marketing sentences compressed into two words. Unpack them and you get a much better idea of whether a machine suits how you actually cook. Three names carry almost all the weight on the dual-basket unit we track.
Two baskets: what “independent” buys, and what it costs

The Chefman page for this model describes a 6-quart air fryer that “combines two powerful air fryers in one, allowing you to cook different dishes simultaneously or easily switch between baskets”. The Amazon listing title is more specific: two independent 3-quart baskets. Independent means two temperatures and two timers. It also means each chamber is 3 quarts, so a batch that would lie flat in one 6-quart drawer now has to be split. Two small baskets and one big basket are different tools that happen to share a word.
Sync Finish is a timing feature, not a cooking feature

The manufacturer describes a Sync Finish feature “to ensure both baskets finish cooking simultaneously”. That is the whole promise: the machine manages when one side starts so two foods land on the table together. It does not equalise temperature between the sides, it does not make a chicken thigh and a tray of fries cook alike, and it will not rescue a dish that needed a different technique. If your Tuesday problem is two things, one plug, same table, it is aimed squarely at that. If your problem is even browning across one large batch, it is not.
Hi-Fry is a number, and the number is disputed

On the dual-basket page the manufacturer states a maximum of 450 °F (235 °C) with the Hi-Fry function, and the listing title lists Hi-Fry among the features. On the 8 qt single-basket Chefman the two official pages disagree: the manufacturer page states a 200-400 °F range for the model, while the Amazon title advertises a 450 °F Hi-Fry option that no page of ours explains. This site publishes the 400 °F figure for that unit and leaves the 450 °F claim named but unadopted, with the disagreement recorded on the Flagged for review page (FLG-027). When two official sources conflict, the conservative figure goes on the page and the conflict goes in the register.

body.text: Three questions to ask of any dual-basket listing

items: What is the capacity of one basket, not of the pair? Compare a single batch against a single chamber, not against a total.
Which page states the temperature ceiling - the maker's specification or the listing title? If they differ, the difference belongs in your decision, not in a footnote.
Is there a care statement about the baskets - nonstick, dishwasher-safe, top rack only? Washing is part of the daily cost of owning this shape, and it is a separate claim from the cooking one.

body.text: No appliance was operated to write this guide. Every feature sentence above is a statement from a manufacturer page or from the observed Amazon listing, and the two are attributed separately because they are not always the same sentence.

items.q: Do I need Sync Finish if I can set a timer myself?
items.a: You can do the same arithmetic by hand. The feature saves you starting one side late and watching two countdowns, which on a busy evening is most of its value.

items.q: Is Hi-Fry worth paying for?
items.a: That cannot be answered from these pages, because they state what the function is - a higher temperature ceiling - and not how it performs. We do not publish a performance opinion we cannot source.

items.q: Can a dual-basket unit replace a single big drawer for a family?
items.a: Only if your batches fit in 3 quarts each. For one large single item, the 8 qt single-basket shape exists for exactly that reason, which is why both shapes stay on our shelf.

guides.title: 24 presets or 25? How to read a preset list
guides.image_alt: Illustration of a countertop oven control panel with a row of blank preset buttons under a blank display
guides.deck: The preset count is the one number on the box that cannot be compared between brands. Here is what to check instead, worked through one machine we actually track.
guides.description: Why preset counts and function counts are not comparable between air fryers, worked through the Emeril Lagasse 26 QT French Door oven, whose own pages state 24 and 25 presets and 10-in-1 and 11-in-1.
guides.summary: The Emeril 26 QT oven states its own preset count two ways: the manufacturer page's specification strip reads 25 cooking pre-sets while that same page's description, and the Amazon listing title, read 24 one-touch presets; the function count appears as 10-in-1 in prose and 11-in-1 in a page image. This site publishes the disagreement rather than a number. The comparable fields are capacity, the maker's own serving line, fan behaviour, outside dimensions, voltage and the accessories actually named.

body.text: A preset count looks like a spec and behaves like a slogan. The number is real - somebody counted buttons - but the unit is arbitrary, because nothing standardises what a preset is. It is the one figure on a box on which two brands cannot be compared, and it is usually the first number a listing leads with.
A worked example, from a machine we actually track

The Emeril Lagasse 26 QT French Door oven states its own preset count two different ways on the same manufacturer page. Its specification strip reads “25 Cooking Pre-sets”. The description on that same page opens “This endlessly versatile 10-in-1 air fry convection oven…”. The Amazon listing title reads “24 One-Touch Preset Options”. And the manufacturer page carries an image whose file name and on-page note record an eleven-function count. Four figures from two official pages about one machine, each of them published somewhere the brand controls.

So what went on the product page? None of them, as a fact. The disagreement is recorded, sourced and dated (FLG-024), and the fields a shopper can act on are the ones both pages agree on. That is this site's whole editorial method in miniature: no reconciliation, no averaging, no quietly picking the friendlier number.
What to read instead of the preset count

headers: Why it compares better than a preset count
rows: Capacity
26 quarts, restated on the same page as 24.6 litres
A volume in a shared unit. Two makers' quarts mean the same thing.
Who it is stated to feed
The manufacturer's own strip pairs the 26-quart capacity with “preparing food for 4-6 people”
A household-size claim is more usable than a cubic measure, and it is the maker's words, not ours.
Fan
Listed as a dual-speed fan “for golden fried crisping”
Fan behaviour is what changes a result; a preset is a stored combination of it.
Outside size
16.9 in deep x 15.8 in wide x 14.8 in high
This decides whether it lives on your counter, and it is comparable across any two boxes.
Electrical
120 volts
The figure you need before deciding where it may be plugged in.
Included accessories
The listing title says six; the description on the same listing mentions seven
Named pieces are checkable; a count is not, when the count disagrees with itself.

body.text: If you still want to judge the presets

Then judge them on the three things that make a preset usable, none of which a count expresses: what temperature and time each preset applies; whether the presets cover the foods you actually cook (wings and roasted vegetables are common, a genuine dehydrate step and a bake step are not universal); and whether you can leave a preset and set time and temperature by hand in two presses. That last one decides whether the panel helps you or gets in your way once you stop cooking from buttons.
No timing, browning or doneness claim appears on this page, because no source we hold supports one. This is a guide to reading a specification sheet, not a review of the appliance.

items.q: Is 25 presets better than 24?
items.a: Neither. There is no common definition of a preset, and here the same manufacturer's page gives both answers depending on which part of it you read. A count can only tell you roughly how much of the panel is shortcuts.

items.q: Should I trust the listing title or the manufacturer page?
items.a: Trust whichever one states the claim you can corroborate elsewhere on the same page, and treat the disagreement as information. Where a claim sits on one page only, this site publishes it as that page's claim - “the maker states…” - and not as a fact about the product.

items.q: What about 10-in-1 versus 11-in-1?
items.a: The same problem one level up: it depends what a company counts as a function. If a specific mode matters to you - dehydrate, proof, rotisserie - look for that mode named with a temperature range, not for a total.

body.text: Every specification on our product pages is shown with the page that states it, and every disagreement between two official pages has its own row in the flag register.
body.label: Read the source register

guides.title: Holiday cooking: what one countertop oven holds
guides.image_alt: Illustration of a countertop air fryer oven with its french doors open beside a roasting pan of vegetables, a cutting board and an open notebook
guides.deck: Before you plan a holiday around a countertop oven, get four numbers straight: who it says it feeds, what it measures outside, what safety requires, and which thermometer you will use.
guides.description: A planning checklist for running a holiday meal through a 26-quart countertop air fryer oven: the manufacturer's capacity and serving statements, outside dimensions, the USDA temperatures that do not bend, and instant-read versus leave-in probes.
guides.summary: The 26-quart Emeril French Door oven we track states its capacity as food for 4-6 people, in 24.6 litres, inside an outside box of 16.9 x 15.8 x 14.8 inches on 120 volts. No page we read states the largest bird that fits inside, so this guide does not estimate one. What it sets out instead: the USDA minimum temperatures that apply whatever heats the food (all poultry 165 °F), checking a large irregular roast in several places, and which of the two probes we track suits the day itself.

body.text: Every November the same advice circulates: put the bird in the air fryer and free up your oven. It can work. It also has three failure points that have nothing to do with technique - fit, food safety and timing - and two of the three can be settled from a specification sheet before you buy anything.
1. Fit: read the maker's serving number, not the quart number

Quarts are hard to picture, so use the manufacturer's own translation. The page for the 26 QT French Door oven we track states “26-Quart Capacity” with the line “preparing food for 4-6 people”, 24.6 litres, and outside dimensions of 16.9 in deep by 15.8 in wide by 14.8 in high. That is a household-size claim from the maker rather than a guess by us, and it is the honest limit of what can be said: none of the official pages we read states the largest bird that fits inside. If a listing tells you a specific weight of poultry fits, ask which page says so.

Then measure the counter, twice. The outside box is what competes with the coffee maker, and clearance is what decides whether the doors can open. A french-door oven is deeper than a basket fryer by design - that is the price of having rack positions.
2. Safety: target temperatures do not change with the appliance

A countertop oven does not get its own food-safety rules. From the USDA chart, the numbers that matter on a holiday: all poultry - breasts, whole bird, legs, thighs, wings, ground poultry, giblets and stuffing - at 165 °F; ground meats 160 °F; beef, pork, veal and lamb steaks, chops and roasts at 145 °F with at least a three-minute rest; leftovers and casseroles reheated to 165 °F. And the measurement is the part people skip: those temperatures are stated “as measured with a food thermometer”.

items: Do not judge by colour. USDA's factsheet is blunt that colour and grill marks are not indicators that food is safe, and cites its own study in which 21% of participants relied on visual cues for hamburger patties.
Check a large or irregularly shaped roast in several places, and check each piece separately - size, quantity and how food is stacked mean pieces reach temperature at different times (FSIS).
Put the probe in the thickest part, away from bone, fat and gristle (FSIS).
Keep perishable food out of the 40-140 °F range for more than two hours (FSIS). On a buffet day that is a serving decision, not a cooking one.

body.text: 3. Timing: which thermometer earns a place at the table

Two shapes of thermometer, two different jobs on the day. A folding instant-read probe - the ThermoMaven row we track states a one-second read on a thermocouple sensor, a 100% waterproof body and a built-in magnet - is a spot check: you walk to the food. A leave-in wireless probe - the CHEF iQ Sense row is described by its maker with four internal sensors plus one ambient sensor and a Wi-Fi hub - watches the food while you are in another room. One person can carry the first through an entire meal. The second earns its keep when something is cooking for hours, or when the appliance sits in a room you keep leaving.
4. The plan, in the order that actually works

items: Write the menu, then write the appliances: what runs in the countertop oven, what runs in the main oven, what only needs reheating.
Give the countertop oven the shortest, least-attended job first. Sides and reheating are where a second chamber pays; the main roast is where an unexpected door opening costs the most.
Decide where the thermometer sits before you start. An ambient probe in a small chamber that gets opened every few minutes will chase its own tail.
Leave one rack position empty. A chamber that is 26 quarts with nothing in it is smaller with three pans and foil in it, and no page states a loaded capacity.
Check temperature in more than one place, rest the meat for the time the chart asks for, and write the numbers down if you are cooking for people you are responsible for.

body.text: This is a planning guide, not a results guide. Nobody on this site cooked a holiday dinner in these machines, so there are no cook times, no crispiness claims and no brining advice. What is here comes from a manufacturer page, the observed listing and USDA FSIS guidance, each listed below.

items.q: Can I cook a whole turkey in a 26-quart countertop oven?
items.a: No page we hold answers that, so neither do we. What we can tell you is what the maker states for that model - food for 4-6 people in 26 quarts - and that the fit question should be answered from a document that names a size or a weight, not from a volume figure.

items.q: Does the air fry function change the safe temperature?
items.a: No. Minimum internal temperatures are the same whatever heats the food, which is why this guide spends its space on measurement rather than on method.

items.q: Do I need a wireless probe for a holiday?
items.a: You need a thermometer. The wireless one buys you the option to leave the room and to watch the ambient temperature as well; an instant-read probe used on every piece does the safety job for a fraction of the price and with no app to open.
